sources.title: Nishi Amane (Q906354), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-13): English label 'Nishi Amane', description 'Japanese philosopher and politician (1829-1897)', instance of human, born 1829-03-07, died 1897-01-30, citizenship Japan, Japanese label 西周, Korean label 니시 아마네. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Gino K. Piovesana, 'Nishi Amane (1829-1897)', Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Gale, 1967; reproduced on Encyclopedia.com; read in full including its bibliography). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: calls him the pioneer who brought Western philosophy to Japan; sent to Holland in 1862, where his interest in philosophy was reawakened and he met Comte's positivism, J. S. Mill's utilitarianism and Kant; the new terminology he created, from tetsugaku to his many translations, and original works that began a tradition of speculative thinking (Reikon ichigenron, Hyakugaku renkan and Hyakuichi shinron of 1874, the first Japanese logic Chichi keimo, the 1875 'three treasures' essay); his translations of Mill's Utilitarianism and Haven's Mental Philosophy; a member of the Meirokusha; later a more conservative attitude, and the judgement that he remained an expositor of Western philosophy who never really tried to combine East and West. Reference-work entry; balanced, and openly limiting.

Nobuo Takayanagi (Gakushuin University), "Japan's 'Isolated Father' of Philosophy: NISHI Amane and His 'Tetsugaku'", University of Tokyo Center for Philosophy (UTCP) publication (read in full). Scholarly analysis: Nishi was a Confucian-trained scholar who studied law, economics and politics at Leiden under Simon Vissering from 1863; in 1873 he gave his reason for coining tetsugaku (to avoid confusing Western philosophy with Neo-Confucian terms); he praised Comte's positivism and its inductive method yet judged that Comte had not integrated the sciences; from 1873 he tried to write 'Seisei hatsuun' to join physiology and psychology into one system, failed, and in 1882 said he lacked the ability, making no further attempt; his view of human nature resembled the Confucian one, and he did not take up Spencer's evolutionary philosophy; his philosophy left no direct descendants although the term 'tetsugaku' survived. Independent, critical-leaning, source-grounded in his collected works.

Yasuhira Kanayama (Nagoya University), 'The Birth of Philosophy as Tetsugaku in Japan', Tetsugaku vol. 1 (2017), Philosophical Association of Japan (read; sections on Nishi in full). Peer-reviewed article: his coinage of tetsugaku and the earlier form kitetsugaku (1861-62), which he dropped within a few years and decided against by 1867 at the latest; he refused Confucian words such as rigaku for it; his 1867 Kyoto lectures on Western law and philosophy for nearly 500 retainers; the private school Ikueisha (1870-c.1873) where he lectured on Hyakugaku renkan, which defines philosophy as 'the science of sciences'; his friend Tsuda Mamichi kept using the older word; Meirokusha (1873) and its successor the Tokyo Academy; the word later entered Chinese through the Tokyo University curriculum. Independent scholarly article, relies on his collected works and Aso Yoshiteru (1942).

Takako Saito, 'The Meaning of Heaven according to Nishi Amane' (Frontiers of Japanese Philosophy; English translation of a French essay; read in full). Scholarly essay on his use of the idea of 'ri' (principle) to clarify European terms: he was qualified to teach Confucianism before leaving his fief in 1854, later criticised Song Neo-Confucianism for not separating politics from morality and for venerating antiquity yet could not shake off its idea of Heaven, was influenced by Ogyu Sorai, translated Vissering, Haven's Mental Philosophy and Mill's Utilitarianism, wrote on psychology, logic, morality, law and politics, and is held to be the first translator of terms such as risei (reason), kannen (idea), shutai (subject), kyakkan (object) and tetsugaku. Independent scholarly essay on one aspect of his thought.

National Diet Library, Japan, 'NISHI Amane', Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures (English and Japanese pages read, short biography). Enlightenment thinker, son of a physician of the Tsuwano domain; studied Confucianism, then Dutch and English in Edo; 1857 junior assistant instructor at the shogunate's Bansho Shirabesho; studied in Holland 1862-65; translated and published 'International Law' in 1868; took part in the Meirokusha and wrote in its journal; held government posts; 'suggested many new terminologies and introduced European philosophy and logic'. Short institutional biography.

National Diet Library, Japan, 'Students Studying in the Netherlands at the End of the Edo Period', Japan-Netherlands Exchange in the Edo Period (read). Records that the shogunate chose Tsuda Mamichi and Nishi Amane from the Bureau for the Inspection of Barbarian Books to study in the Netherlands in April 1862, that the group left Edo in July 1862, survived a shipwreck off Sumatra in November, reached Leiden in June 1863 and that Nishi and Tsuda returned first, on 1 December 1865; includes a 1865 group photograph. Institutional history page; the study trip was assigned by the shogunate.

Esben Andreasen and David Mark Larsson, 'Amane Nishi', Lex (Den Store Danske; read in Danish). Short encyclopedia entry: sent to Leiden in 1862 for economics, law and political science but drawn to philosophy, positivism and Mill's utilitarianism; originator of several Japanese words for Western concepts including tetsugaku and the word for jurisprudence; critical of Confucianism except Ogyu Sorai; and the judgement that today the interest in him is mainly historical and that apart from the word for philosophy he is not regarded as a weighty contributor to modern Japanese philosophy. Brief reference entry, useful as a counter-voice.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_nishi_saito, src_nishi_eop, src_nishi_kanayama, src_nishi_ndl | 1854-1880s | scholarly essays, reference entry, national library biography] He moved from Confucian studies to Dutch and English, then law, economics and politics at Leiden, and wrote on psychology, logic, morality, law and politics (Saito); the Encyclopedia of Philosophy adds his logic text, his ethics and his positivist monism; Kanayama describes the Hyakugaku renkan lectures as an encyclopedia of the sciences, philosophy, theology and law; the library biography lists international law, logic and philosophy. The range is documented by several sources, but all lie within the humanities and social sciences.

curiosity.rationale: [src_nishi_eop, src_nishi_saito, src_nishi_kanayama | 1854-1867 | reference entry, scholarly essays] He learned Dutch and English in Edo from 1854, wrote in 1862 to a friend that Western learning on human nature and political economy contained 'astonishingly great theories' (Takayanagi, Kanayama), and in Holland read Comte, Mill and Kant (Encyclopedia of Philosophy). The 1862 Leiden study was assigned by the shogunate, so the interest in philosophy rather than the assigned law is the personal signal; the sources are scholarly reconstructions from his letters and notes.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_nishi_saito, src_nishi_kanayama, src_nishi_ndl, src_nishi_ndl_nichiran | 1854-1877 | scholarly essays, library biography, institutional history] Nominated a teacher of Confucian studies in his domain in 1854, he learned Dutch and English, was made a junior instructor at the shogunate's institute in 1857, studied under Vissering at Leiden in 1863-65, translated Vissering's lectures, Haven's Mental Philosophy and Mill's Utilitarianism, and lectured on Western law and philosophy from 1867. The sequence of study, translation and teaching is documented across four sources, but the Leiden study was a shogunate assignment and the sources do not describe how he worked. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.54 to 64 / 0.48 because mastery is read indirectly from an official career path.

belief_updating.rationale: [src_nishi_kanayama, src_nishi_takayanagi, src_nishi_saito | 1862-1882 | scholarly articles] After Western study he criticised Neo-Confucianism, the school he had been trained in (Saito); he dropped his first coinage kitetsugaku for tetsugaku within a few years and refused Confucian vocabulary (Kanayama); and from 1873 he tried to unify physiology and psychology in one system, failed and in 1882 said he lacked the ability, making no later attempt (Takayanagi). Three distinct episodes, but Saito and Kanayama draw on the same collected works and Takayanagi's failure account is one scholar's reading. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.50 to 62 / 0.44 because the three episodes are narrated through the same editions of his papers and the abandoned-system claim rests on one article.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_nishi_eop, src_nishi_kanayama, src_nishi_saito, src_nishi_takayanagi, src_nishi_lex | 1862-1877 | reference entry, scholarly articles, encyclopedia entry] He coined tetsugaku (decided by 1867 at the latest), and is held to be the first translator of risei, kannen, shutai and kyakkan (Saito); the Encyclopedia of Philosophy credits his new terminology and a first Japanese logic text. The ideas themselves were drawn from Comte, Mill and Haven and the same entry calls him an expositor, Lex says his interest is mainly historical, and Takayanagi says his philosophy had no direct descendants. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.50 to 60 / 0.44 because the 'father of Japanese philosophy' reputation partly rests on the lasting success of his coinages (outcome bias) while the scholarly judgements of his own ideas are lukewarm.

systems_abstraction.rationale: [src_nishi_takayanagi, src_nishi_kanayama, src_nishi_eop | 1867-1882 | scholarly articles, reference entry] His Hyakugaku renkan lectures arranged the sciences into a scheme with philosophy as the 'science of sciences' (Kanayama); Takayanagi shows him analysing Comte's system for its missing link between physiology and psychology and trying to join them in 'Seisei hatsuun', which he did not finish; the Encyclopedia of Philosophy describes panoramic treatments of Western learning. The attempt at an integrating system is well documented, and its non-completion is why the impact is dual-edged.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_nishi_kanayama, src_nishi_eop, src_nishi_ndl | 1867-1879 | scholarly article, reference entry, library biography] He lectured on Western law and philosophy in Kyoto in 1867 to nearly 500 retainers, ran the private school Ikueisha in 1870-c.1873, was one of the main members of the Meirokusha formed in 1873 and wrote for its journal, and the library biography says he introduced European philosophy and logic and suggested many new terms; Kanayama says he intended to introduce the whole system of Western studies. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.50 to 62 / 0.44 because the teaching and school facts come from one article's notes on the Ōkubo and Asō editions and the stated aim is that article's paraphrase.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_nishi_kanayama, src_nishi_eop, src_nishi_saito | 1870-1879 | scholarly article, reference entry, scholarly essay] He established the private school Ikueisha in 1870 for his lectures, was one of the main members of the Meirokusha when it formed in 1873, and was among the founding members of the Tokyo Academy in 1879 (Kanayama, Saito, Encyclopedia of Philosophy). Each is a brief dated mention; no source describes how he started them or what he risked, so this stays an inference.

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (lead) / lead SURVIVED in substance. The lead was Commons 'Nishi Amane.jpg' (523x671, cited as from the 1933 Iwanami Nishi Amane tetsugaku chosakushu via NDL Portraits datas/309, PD-Japan-oldphoto); the portrait used is the National Diet Library's own file for the same photograph (NDL Portraits 0309_1.jpg, 1281x1760, downscaled to 728x1000), which is higher quality than the Commons extract and is the holder's own copy. HOLDER RECORD: the NDL Digital Collections item record for pid 1176475 (Nishi Amane tetsugaku chosakushu, Iwanami Shoten, 1933, 405p with portrait; exhibit tag 'Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures: Nishi Amane', link to the Portraits page) was read through the NDL item API: permission rule 'ooc' (out of copyright), search and OAI allowed, rights code empty (not 'undetermined'). The NDL page images of the book require sign-in (HTTP 401) and were not retrieved; the NDL Portraits site statement was not relied on. Basis: photograph published in Japan in 1933 by an unknown photographer; a photograph first published in Japan before 1 January 1958 is public domain in Japan and in the United States (not restored by the URAA; Commons template PD-Japan-oldphoto). SITTER IDENTITY: the NDL Portraits page for NISHI Amane presents this image as his portrait, and the same photograph (correlation 0.96 on a downscaled comparison) is on Commons as 'Portrait of Mr. Amane Nishi (taken in 1880)', transcribed from the same 1933 book with the plate caption 西周先生肖影（明治13年6月写）; I could not read the printed caption in the book, so the 1880 date is carried only as a transcription. The other NDL image of him (0309_2, a coarse halftone of an older man in kimono) was not used. KIND likeness: a photograph of the sitter, taken in his lifetime per the plate caption (not independently confirmed). The embossed NDL stamp is faintly visible at lower left. ZERO POLITICS: only scholarship, translation, teaching and intellectual institution-building are scored; his posts in the Army-Navy Ministry, the Chamber of Elders and the House of Peers, his army-reform writings and his barony are context only and unscored (the Wikidata description lists 'politician'). VOCABULARY: occupations philosopher, scholar, teacher; fields philosophy, education; impact domains cultural, educational, historical; tags philosopher, communicator, systematic_thinker; archetype scholarly_specialist. ATTRIBUTION: attributable (dated lectures, coined terms, translations, documented works). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Piovesana, Nishi Amane, Encyclopedia of Philosophy (1967) via Encyclopedia.com. READ (7 sources besides Wikidata): Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry (full); Takayanagi (full); Kanayama (Nishi sections in full); Saito (first sections, English essay); NDL Portraits biography (English and Japanese); NDL Japan-Netherlands exchange page; Lex entry. Also opened but not cited: the Journal of Asian Studies page for Hackett's 1959 article (only the extract and references were visible), Britannica (403), a Chinese-language PDF on his translation of political economy (text not readable), a Leiden thesis page (not readable); Wikipedia not used. Not opened: Havens's 1970 book, Koizumi's 1989 study, Okubo's collected works. PERSPECTIVES: (1) reference-work biography (Piovesana); (2) critical scholarly analysis of his system and its failure (Takayanagi); (3) intellectual-history article on his coinage of tetsugaku (Kanayama); (4) essay on his terminology and Confucian inheritance (Saito); (5) institutional biographies; (6) a short Danish encyclopedia entry with a deflating judgement. NON-SELF BEHAVIOURAL SOURCES: all of the above; the scholarly articles quote his letters, notes and works, so part of the behavioural detail is his own words filtered through scholars, and the three journal-style sources largely rely on one set of editions of his collected works (Okubo, Aso). LIMITS: no adversarial biography was found; the sources disagree on emphasis (father of Japanese philosophy versus a historically interesting expositor); his Leiden study and many posts were assigned by the shogunate and later governments; no health, family or private-life evidence is used. Sparse 8-row profile by design; no rows on persistence, discipline, collaboration or risk because the sources do not describe them. MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT GATE PASS: cards (1) coining tetsugaku and the vocabulary of Western thought, (2) introducing Western philosophy, logic and positivism through his writings and lectures, (3) the Meirokusha and the Tokyo Academy. SELF-CALIBRATION: lowered belief_updating, impact_motivation (concentration), creative_originality and mastery_orientation (self-calibration), see handback; no raise flags.
